This soldier kept fighting World War Two for twenty-nine years after it ended. And it took a backpacker and an old bookseller to stop him.
In 1944, Japan sent Lieutenant Hiroo Onoda to a jungle island in the Philippines. His orders: never surrender.
A year later, the war ended. But nobody could convince him.
Planes dropped leaflets saying the war was over. He decided they were enemy tricks.
So he stayed. For decades, he and his men raided farms for food, and their raids killed about thirty islanders.
One by one, his men surrendered or died. By 1972, he was alone.
Then in 1974, a young Japanese backpacker named Norio Suzuki went looking for him. His list: Onoda, a panda, and the Yeti.
He found Onoda in four days.
But Onoda still refused to give up. Only his commanding officer could order that.
So Suzuki flew home, and tracked down that officer. He was now a bookseller.
The old man flew to the island, and read Onoda his new orders. The war is over.
Onoda saluted, and finally handed over his sword.
